title: Hold an answer back without holding up the connection

blocks.text: A `late=1500` rule is fine for a person trying things by hand, but an automated test that needs an answer to arrive *after* the client gave up depends on the machine being fast enough. On a loaded build server the test fails now and then. QA wants the host to keep an answer back until the test says "now", whatever the clock does.
`HoldingHost` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/HoldingHost.java` approves every request, and it is given the STANs whose answers the test wants to hold. Two methods are `TODO`:

items: `hold(client, answer)`: keep the answer until the test releases it.
`release()`: the test calls it from its own thread. It sends the answers held so far and returns how many reached a client.

blocks.text: `process` is called the way `ISOServer` calls it. A test may hold several answers, from several clients, before it releases them, and a client may disconnect while its answer is held. The tests call `process` and `release` from different threads. About 12 lines in total.

cases.says: a request whose STAN is not held is approved at once, and a release with nothing held sends nothing
the answer to a held request reaches the client once the test releases it
holding an answer returns from process at once, so the next request on the same connection is answered while the first waits
release sends the held answers in the order their requests arrived, including two clients with the same STAN
a held answer whose client has gone, before or during the send, is skipped, and the others are still sent and counted
answers held by several sessions while the test releases from its own thread are each sent exactly once
a released answer is not sent again by a later release

origin.section: 16.2 A Listener Runs on the Session's Thread, So a Late Answer Is Scheduled

concepts: ISOServer calls listeners on the session's thread, so a listener that waits delays every later request on that connection; a late answer is handed off and process returns.
